captions.text: Okay, I've got the projectile-motion notes up. We start from Newton's second law. Split into horizontal and vertical. The two directions are uncoupled, so gravity acts only on y. That means the horizontal acceleration is zero, and the vertical acceleration is minus g. We integrate each one to get velocity and then position. So x increases linearly with time, while y picks up the minus g over 2 t squared term. Putting them together, you eliminate time and get a parabola in x. No. Once you add drag, the symmetry breaks, and the best angle is usually less than 45 degrees. How much less depends on the shape, speed, and how strong the drag is.

No, the height is maximized when you shoot straight up, theta ninety degrees, because the vertical component is then largest. The 45 degree result is only about maximizing horizontal range with no air resistance, not about height.

They give the same range because the formula has sine of 2 theta, and sine doesn't change if you swap theta with 90 minus theta. So 30 and 60 share the same sine of 2 theta. What's different is the split between horizontal and vertical speed. At 30, you have more horizontal speed and less hang time, so a flatter arc. At 60, you go higher, stay up longer, but move forward more slowly, so you land at the same distance.
